query: For high-entropy alloys, what single intervention could improve hardness and strength without sacrificing useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, the mechanism expected to produce the improvement, a measurable outcome relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with clear observations that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a small amount of molybdenum (Mo) to high-entropy alloys can improve hardness and strength without sacrificing useful mechanical performance.
generation.intervention: Addition of molybdenum (Mo) in small amounts (1–3 wt %)
generation.conditions: Annealing at 500 °C for 3 h and air-cooling
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a single FCC solid solution with possible precipitation of σ phase at higher Mo content
generation.mechanism: Solid solution strengthening and possible precipitation hardening due to the formation of σ phase
generation.predicted_outcome: Increased hardness and compressive yield strength without fracture under ~60% strain
generation.uncertainty: The effect of Mo addition on corrosion resistance, particularly in chloride environments, is uncertain and requires further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare high-entropy alloy (CoCrFeNi)100−xMox with x = 0, 1, 2, and 3 wt % and test their mechanical properties (hardness and compressive yield strength) and corrosion resistance in chloride environments
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Mo does not result in increased hardness and compressive yield strength, or if it significantly deteriorates corrosion resistance in chloride environments, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How does the addition of molybdenum (Mo) in small amounts (1–3 wt %) affect the microstructure, mechanical properties, and corrosion behavior of (CoCrFeNi)100−xMox high-entropy alloys in chloride and acidic environments?. System: (CoCrFeNi)100−xMox with x = 1, 2, and 3 wt % (designated Mo1, Mo2, Mo3). Processing: Vacuum arc melting using elements with >99.9 wt % purity, melted at least five times in a WK-∏ furnace; ingots (Φ 35 × 10 mm) annealed for 3 h at 500 °C and air-cooled. Test conditions: Microhardness (500 g load, 10 s); compressive tests (Φ 3 × 6 mm, strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹); electrochemical tests in 3.5% NaCl and 0.5 M H2SO4 at room temperature; potentiodynamic polarization scan rate 1 mV/s from −0.5 V to 1.1 V vs. SCE. Findings: All alloys exhibit a single FCC solid solution, except Mo3 which contains a Cr- and Mo-rich σ phase in interdendrites.; Hardness increases from 124.8 HV (Mo1) to 133.6 HV (Mo3) as Mo content rises from 1 to 3 wt %.; Compressive yield strength increases from 113.6 MPa (Mo1) to 141.1 MPa (Mo3) without fracture under ~60% strain.; In 3.5% NaCl, Mo3 shows a corrosion current density (icorr) of 6.6 μA/cm², an order of magnitude high
